\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{ناامید} (nâomid)}{ناامید (nâomid)}]{\fa{ناامید} (nâomid) — disappointed; hopeless}

\label{lesson:FA-C487-naomid}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for love, then the Persian for to hate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{ناامید}}
\textbf{\fa{ناامید}} (\emph{nâomid}) — \textquotedblleft{}disappointed; hopeless\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{او} \fa{از} \fa{نتیجه} \fa{امتحان} \fa{ناامید} \fa{شد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{u az natije-ye emtehân nâomid shod.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
He was disappointed with the exam result.
\end{quote}

\emph{nâ-} 'not' + \emph{omid} 'hope'. The noun is \emph{nâomidi}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nâomid} is built on native Persian pieces: the prefix \emph{nâ-}, 'not', and \emph{omid}, 'hope', which is usually traced to Middle Persian \emph{ummēd}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nâomid}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nâomid}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{nâomid}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Persian for love, then the Persian for to hate, then say \emph{nâomid} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \fa{ناامید} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Disappointed; hopeless\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{خوشبین} (khoshbin)}{خوشبین (khoshbin)}]{\fa{خوشبین} (khoshbin) — optimistic}

\label{lesson:FA-C487-khoshbin}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for to hate, then the Persian for disappointed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{خوشبین}}
\textbf{\fa{خوشبین}} (\emph{khoshbin}) — \textquotedblleft{}optimistic\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{پدرم} \fa{همیشه} \fa{به} \fa{آینده} \fa{خوشبین} \fa{است}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{pedaram hamishe be âyande khoshbin ast.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My father is always optimistic about the future.
\end{quote}

\emph{khosh} 'good' + \emph{bin} 'seeing' (stem of \emph{didan}). What you are hopeful about takes \emph{be}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{khoshbin} is built on native Persian parts: \emph{khosh}, 'good, pleasant', and \emph{bin}, the present stem of \emph{didan}, 'to see': someone who sees things well.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Persian for to hate, then the Persian for disappointed, then say \emph{khoshbin} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{بدبین} (badbin)}{بدبین (badbin)}]{\fa{بدبین} (badbin) — pessimistic; distrustful}

\label{lesson:FA-C487-badbin}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for disappointed, then the Persian for optimistic.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{بدبین}}
\textbf{\fa{بدبین}} (\emph{badbin}) — \textquotedblleft{}pessimistic; distrustful\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{او} \fa{به} \fa{همه} \fa{بدبین} \fa{است}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{u be hame badbin ast.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
He distrusts everyone.
\end{quote}

\emph{bad} 'bad' + \emph{bin} 'seeing'. \emph{be kasi badbin budan} — to distrust someone.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{badbin} is built on native Persian \emph{bad}, 'bad', and \emph{bin}, the present stem of \emph{didan}, 'to see'. Persian \emph{bad} looks like English \emph{bad}, but they are not related.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{اعتماد} \fa{به} \fa{نفس} (e'temâd be nafs)}{اعتماد به نفس (e'temâd be nafs)}]{\fa{اعتماد} \fa{به} \fa{نفس} (e'temâd be nafs) — self-confidence}

\label{lesson:FA-C487-etemad-be-nafs}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for optimistic, then the Persian for pessimistic.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{اعتماد} \fa{به} \fa{نفس}}
\textbf{\fa{اعتماد} \fa{به} \fa{نفس}} (\emph{e'temâd be nafs}) — \textquotedblleft{}self-confidence\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{او} \fa{بعد} \fa{از} \fa{این} \fa{مسابقه} \fa{اعتماد} \fa{به} \fa{نفس} \fa{بیشتری} \fa{دارد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{u ba'd az in mosâbeqe e'temâd be nafs-e bishtari dârad.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
After this contest he has more self-confidence.
\end{quote}

\emph{e'temâd} 'trust' + \emph{be} 'in' + \emph{nafs} 'self': trust in oneself.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{e'temâd be nafs} is built in Persian from two Arabic loans: \emph{e'temâd}, usually traced to Arabic \emph{iʿtimād}, 'reliance', and \emph{nafs}, borrowed from Arabic \emph{nafs}, 'self, soul' (EtymDB), joined by Persian \emph{be}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{e'temâd be nafs}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{e'temâd be nafs}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Persian for optimistic, then the Persian for pessimistic, then say \emph{e'temâd be nafs} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{شجاعت} (shojâ'at)}{شجاعت (shojâ'at)}]{\fa{شجاعت} (shojâ'at) — courage, bravery}

\label{lesson:FA-C487-shojaat}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for pessimistic, then the Persian for self-confidence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{شجاعت}}
\textbf{\fa{شجاعت}} (\emph{shojâ'at}) — \textquotedblleft{}courage, bravery\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{آتش} \fa{نشان} \fa{با} \fa{شجاعت} \fa{بچه} \fa{را} \fa{نجات} \fa{داد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{âtashneshân bâ shojâ'at bachche râ nejât dâd.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The firefighter bravely saved the child.
\end{quote}

\emph{bâ shojâ'at} — bravely. The adjective is \emph{shojâ'} 'brave'.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{shojâ'at} is a loan, usually traced to Arabic \emph{šajāʿa}, 'courage'. Its partner \emph{shojâ'}, 'brave', was borrowed from Arabic \emph{šujāʿ} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{shojâ'at}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Persian for pessimistic, then the Persian for self-confidence, then say \emph{shojâ'at} again
